# apache/skywalking#14092: [Feature] BanyanDB: local-scan performance follow-up for tag aggregation (optional)
State: open. Labels: feature, database. https://github.com/apache/skywalking/issues/14092

Part 5 of 5 of the [tag aggregation and time bucketing design](https://github.com/apache/skywalking-banyandb/blob/main/docs/design/0.12.0/tag-aggregation/README.md), shipped in apache/skywalking-banyandb#1360.

**Design references:** [§7.7 The local scan: entity and indexed tags never touch the data file](https://github.com/apache/skywalking-banyandb/blob/main/docs/design/0.12.0/tag-aggregation/README.md#77-the-local-scan-entity-and-indexed-tags-never-touch-the-data-file) · [§12 Delivery order](https://github.com/apache/skywalking-banyandb/blob/main/docs/design/0.12.0/tag-aggregation/README.md#12-delivery-order) (stages 8a–9, both marked *optional* in the design)

**Depends on:** #14089 (time-bucket grouping) and #14090 (COUNT_DISTINCT) — this optimizes both. Not required for either to ship; the design explicitly defers this and asks that the payoff be measured before it's built.

## Scope

**Phase A — run-folding** (design's "intermediate step," no new execution path)
- Fold each maximal `(series, bucket)` span once instead of per row, using a plan-time flag marking which key columns are index-resolved — derived from `searchSeriesList`'s existing three-way projection split, never inferred at runtime by sampling column values.
- Applies whenever an index-resolved tag is a group key: `COUNT_DISTINCT` collapses `n − 1` redundant set inserts per span into one; `COUNT` becomes `count += spanLength`.

**Phase B — metadata-only scan** (after Phase A lands)
- Bypass block decode entirely when *every* tag the query touches (group keys, aggregation target, any tag a residual predicate touches) resolves from the series index — gated by the range-containment guard (a block whose `[min,max]` isn't fully inside the query range must still read `timestamps.bin`) and the no-residual-predicate guard.
- `index_mode` measures are the structural first case: they hold no part-resident tags at all, so an index-mode aggregation is index-only by construction.

## Out of scope
- Anything that changes correctness or the query surface — this issue is pure performance, gated by differential tests against the existing (already-correct) path.

## Test / Definition of done
- Phase A: differential test against the unoptimized per-row path on the same fixture (identical results, fewer group-map probes); a magnitude assertion (an 8192-row block at hour buckets collapses to ~137 spans, not 8192 key computations).
- Phase B: differential test against the decoding path across both index-mode and part-backed fixtures (identical results); the range-containment fixture — a block with rows at 09:00 and 09:59 (one hourly bucket) queried over 09:30–09:31 must yield no bucket row, while the same block fully inside the query range takes the shortcut.

# BanyanDB Agent Guide

BanyanDB is a distributed time-series database written in Go. Follow nearby code
and tests; keep changes focused on the requested behavior.

## Completion and scope

- Finish the requested change and relevant verification without asking about
  routine next steps. Stop when the requested outcome is verified or a concrete
  blocker requires user input; do not expand into unrelated fixes or redesigns.
- Preserve unrelated working-tree changes. Do not commit, push, publish, or change
  external resources unless requested or already authorized.
- Use independent subagents when their work saves time; small tasks do not need
  delegation or a separate review workflow.

## Go conventions

- `.golangci.yml` is authoritative for lint rules, protobuf import aliases,
  exclusions, and the 170-character line limit. `.golangci-format.yml` controls
  formatting with gci and gofumpt; its exclusions are not general lint exclusions.
- Import groups: standard library, third-party packages, then this repository.
- Avoid shadowing existing variables. Short names and `if err := ...` are valid
  when they do not shadow another variable; use descriptive names where useful.
- Check errors and add meaningful context with `%w` when wrapping. Preserve error
  identity and the relevant API's error-handling conventions.
- Document exported functions and types with concise, punctuated comments. Add
  implementation comments only for non-obvious logic.

## Correctness and validation

- Follow existing test conventions and run the smallest relevant suites first.
  Expand validation for affected integration boundaries, generated code, or shared
  infrastructure; avoid unrelated full builds during read-only or wording tasks.
- Preserve persisted-data and wire compatibility. For format, schema, or protocol
  changes, check existing data and mixed-version behavior as applicable.
- For concurrent or stateful changes, consider cancellation, resource ownership,
  bounded memory, and recovery. Use the repository's established helpers.
- Read design documents only for the subsystem or contract being changed. Follow
  any more-specific `AGENTS.md` in the affected directory.

- [Tag names are globally unique](project_tag_name_uniqueness.md) — maintainer-confirmed invariant, but NO validator enforces it and the vectorized analyzer assumes the opposite (per-family)
- [BydbQL nested-paren stack-overflow DoS](project_bydbql_paren_depth_dos.md) — FIXED via maxParenDepth guard in pkg/bydbql/parser.go; found but left OPEN a distinct O(n²) participle Unquote DoS on long string literals
- [Vectorized stream query plan](project_vectorized_stream_query_plan.md) — approved-but-unbuilt ralplan (.omc/plans/vectorized-stream-query.md, branch vectorized-stream); native columnar + shared-base wire frame; single PR M1–M7; execution deferred
- [Vectorized trace query pull redesign](project_vectorized_trace_query_pull_redesign.md) — approved-but-unbuilt plan (.omc/plans/vectorized-trace-query.md) to convert trace+sidx query push→pull vectorized; streaming itersort merge, two-phase, 13 ops
- [Dynamic sampler registration plan](project_dynamic_sampler_registration_plan.md) — approved-but-unbuilt ralplan (.omc/plans/dynamic-register-sampler.md) for runtime register/update/remove of trace retention samplers w/o restart; ride KindTrace watch via embedded databasev1.Trace field (a1), B-minus defer RPC, never-Close, blocking US-000 gate
- [Trace sampling skip-marks plan](project_trace_sampling_skip_marks_plan.md) — approved-but-unbuilt ralplan (.omc/plans/trace-sampling-skip-marks.md, branch trace-sampling-perf); no-sample mark is CORE-DERIVED from Verdict.Keep (SDK UNCHANGED, no ABI bump — 2 pivots dropped the plugin field); guard: derive only on !failedOpen not execErr (circuit-open returns nil); mark-aware rawFastPathEligible skips decode; DD7 finalize metadata-only gen-advance
- [User wants a separate mountable plugin image](feedback_user_wants_separate_plugin_image.md) — ship plugins as a separate carrier image mounted into the host, NOT baked in; don't let elegance args override the stated deployment shape
- [Plugin packaging, management & dev-toolkit plan](project_plugin_packaging_management_plan.md) — consensus-APPROVED-but-unbuilt 2-part ralplan (.omc/plans/plugin-packaging-management.md, branch plugin-packaging). PART I: static host CAN'T load Go plugins → bake first-party .so into a single CGO -plugins image (parity by construction), mount only for third-party on /plugins/thirdparty subdir; separate CI job; Helm = follow-up PR to external repo. PART II dev toolkit: share helpers into sdk (EncodeTagValue/OpenSampler/EvaluateChain-with-onBypass, no ABI bump) → sdktest kit (differential projection guard) + banyand-plugin CLI + wire the DEAD per-decision metrics + single-hook dry-run + deep-copy capture + conformance drift guard
- [Vectorized tag-filter limit pushdown](project_vectorized_tag_filter_limit_pushdown.md) — vec trace_tag_filter was 2.3x slower than row from eager full-match materialization; fixed via Phase-1 maxRows cap; QuerySync over-fetch trim still pending
- [Trace native wire format](project_trace_native_wire_format.md) — native wire frame for trace data↔liaison: InternalTrace-shaped frame was NEGATIVE (additive), but COLUMNAR frame aligned with model.TraceResult is POSITIVE — vec beats row (p50 0.82x, −15%, fewer allocs); gated by BANYAND_TRACE_NATIVE_WIRE
- [Matrix B trace bench results](project_matrix_b_trace_bench_results.md) — 1M-span deep dive (2026-06-24): tag_filter vec uniformly faster; by_id "data_nodes=4 regression" was 50-iter NOISE (disproved by 3000-iter reprofile: vec≈row); fan-out cost is gRPC transport, symmetric row/vec; heavytail passes exact correctness; plan stale (impl'd #1182)
- [Soak trace vec query plan](project_soak_trace_vec_query_plan.md) — IMPLEMENTED via ralph 2026-06-25 (uncommitted): TWO-instrument soak (container correctness+survival via SOAK_ENGINE=trace; in-process go-test DQB_SOAK for authoritative QueryCount/leak/budget gates). The soak FOUND & FIXED a real engine leak: BytesBlockDecoder backing-array retained in pooled cursors (block.go reset + sidx releaseBlockCursor); budget heap growth 57%→2.16%
- [Vectorized trace single PR strategy](project_vectorized_trace_single_pr.md) — M1–M7 ships as one PR; CI only on PRs not pushes
- [Trace generated test cases](project_trace_generated_test_cases.md) — trace equivalent of measure's program-generated test framework; engine fixes merged (PR #1147), framework submitted as PR #1150
- [Flaky trace merge metadata test](project_flaky_trace_merge_metadata_test.md) — `metadata_test.go:389` "changed tag type after merge" was timing-flaky under CI/slow-IO; RESOLVED in PR #1147 by scaling merge-wait to 3× EventuallyTimeout
- [Flaky measure snapshot tests](flaky_measure_snapshot_tests.md) — TestSnapshotFunctionality / TestMeasureInitTSTableDeletesMultipleFailedSnapshotsOnFallback gate on part-dir existence (created at start of mustFlush) instead of flush introduction/persist; race repro'd 100% by dropping the sleep
- [Lifecycle meter integration facts](project_lifecycle_meter_cluster_facts.md) — live-cluster topology + code facts for wiring pkg/meter into the lifecycle sidecar (fodc-agent already scrapes :17915; native must target local data node 127.0.0.1:17912)
- [Metric service global host gauges race](project_metric_service_global_host_gauges_race.md) — host gauges + MetricsCollector are process-global; a 2nd in-process metric service (lifecycle sidecar) races under -race while Ginkgo still shows green; fixed via serveWithoutListener (PR #1164)
- [Showcase shadow liaison for UI](project_showcase_shadow_liaison.md) — deploy an unlabeled liaison in live skywalking-showcase GKE + port-forward to use the UI; cluster uses DNS-SRV discovery (no etcd), property schema registry, no TLS
- [Flaky stream deleted-tag encode test](flaky_stream_deleted_tag_encode_test.md) — stream "querying data should succeed after a tag is deleted" (metadata_test.go:389) flaky-panics in CI on int64 tag encode (`expected 8 bytes, got 7`) in the write path under --race; passes locally; unrelated to read-path PRs → re-run the job
- [Flaky backup/dump sidx-snapshot tests](flaky_backup_dump_sidx_snapshot_tests.md) — Test Banyand `.snp` "unexpected end of JSON" snapshot flake ROOT-CAUSED + FIXED in PR #1190: `NoFsyncFS.WriteAtomic` was non-atomic (in-place O_TRUNC) → partial-read panic; now temp+rename
- [Canopy subproject plan](project_canopy_subproject_plan.md) — approved-but-unbuilt ralplan (.omc/plans/canopy-subproject.md) for new `canopy/` subproject: standalone React SPA + Node Fastify BFF implementing the Canopy UI design handoff; no liaison embed, don't touch `ui/`
- [Canopy: read handoff before implementing UI](feedback_canopy_handoff_first.md) — always read `.handoff-import/banyandb/project/` files first; never invent icons, layouts, or CSS from scratch
- [Flaky canopy form unit tests](flaky_canopy_form_unit_tests.md) — RESOLVED 2026-06-29: MeasureForm/Trace/Stream vitest flake (userEvent.type vs sync submit race) fixed by switching fills to fireEvent.change; 145/145 deterministic
- [Generated-test: predict, do not reconcile](feedback_generated_test_predict_not_reconcile.md) — generator predicts expected emptiness from deterministic seed; capture verifies & fails on mismatch; never silently trust the live result
- [Flaky standalone/query integration BeforeSuite](flaky_standalone_query_integration_beforesuite.md) — property-fixture seed fails under host CPU saturation; == main, not trace/branch
- [Flaky schema clamp multi-group query](flaky_schema_clamp_multigroup_query.md) — distributed clamp.go "group not found" on group2 topology race; AwaitRevision confirms schema cache not query topology; fixed w/ gm.Eventually retry (PR #1219)
- [Canopy testing redesign](project_canopy_testing_redesign.md) — E2E framework redesign scaffold landed (framework/ POM+fixtures, seed factory, storageState auth, playwright.next.config, TESTING.md); phased migration + .mjs-probe deletion pending
- [Canopy Property MP design](project_canopy_property_mp.md) — MP milestone design (canopy/docs/property-design.md, branch canopy-property): collection schema via database/v1 registry, documents via property/v1 Apply/Delete/Query, reduced QueryConsole reuse (FROM locked, no TIME), query via structured Query RPC
- [Canopy Pipelines/TopN design](project_canopy_pipelines_topn.md) — Pipelines milestone design (canopy/docs/pipelines-design.md, branch canopy-top): TopN aggregation CRUD via database/v1 TopNAggregationRegistryService; port pipelines.jsx/topn-page.jsx/topn-form.jsx; reuse M3 forms + M4 TopN query; topn-results already = TopNResultView
- [Flaky stream snapshot fallback test](flaky_stream_snapshot_fallback_test.md) — TestStreamTolerantLoaderFallbackToOlderSnapshot flakes on async snapshot-flush timing; re-run, not a real failure
- [Flaky trace snapshot fallback test](flaky_trace_snapshot_fallback_test.md) — TestTraceInitTSTableDeletesMultipleFailedSnapshotsOnFallback, trace sibling of the measure/stream family; plus the `go list -deps` trick proving a plugin-only diff can't break banyand/
- [Trace blockMetadata format break (#1237)](project_trace_blockmetadata_format_break.md) — unversioned primary.bin encoding change broke showcase upgrade; merge-error orphan-dir leak → inode exhaustion → merge lanes wedged
- [Flakes are usually already fixed elsewhere](flaky_tests_already_fixed_elsewhere.md) — check for an existing fix in a sibling package before raising a timeout; 3 of 4 flakes in PR #1268 were unported fixes or misdiagnosed causes
- [bydbctl planner ↔ tool schema coupling](project_bydbctl_planner_tool_schema_coupling.md) — planner capabilities are silently unreachable unless plan_schema.go's tool contract is updated too
- [codex exec pipe hang](codex_exec_pipe_hang.md) — never pipe codex into tail/head (app-server holds the pipe open, hangs forever); --base and a custom prompt are mutually exclusive

})
<commentary>
The agent starts with no context from this conversation, so the prompt briefs it: what to assess, the relevant background, and what form the answer should take.
</commentary>
</example>

tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.

- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

schema.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

content.content:
1	# Tag Aggregation and Time Bucketing in the Measure Query Engine
2	
3	Status: **design** — not implemented.
4	
5	This document specifies three additions to BanyanDB's existing measure query engine:
6	
7	1. aggregation over **tags**, not just fields;
8	2. an exact **`COUNT_DISTINCT`** function;
9	3. **time-bucket grouping** — `GROUP BY <bucket>, <tags>` producing a series, with the bucket
10	   width taken from the request or, failing that, from the measure's `interval`.
11	
12	They are separable features that share one API surface and one operator, and a dashboard needs
13	all three: (1) and (2) answer "how many distinct things", (3) answers "over time".
14	
15	(3) is driven by a separate requirement — converting analytical `GROUP BY <bucket>, <tags>` SQL
16	onto BanyanDB (§1.1) — not by the cardinality work. That conversion also needs two things this
17	document scopes out, multiple aggregates per request and result aliases; §3 records the gap.
18	
19	It is a companion to the [native inverted-index design](../native-inverted-index/README.md): the
20	scoping work for that package asked whether the native index should grow its own local
21	aggregation, and concluded it should not. Aggregation stays in the query engine, which already
22	reduces locally on data nodes and combines at the liaison; this design extends that machinery
23	rather than duplicating it.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 1. Motivation
28	
29	Dashboards built on SkyWalking-shaped measures routinely need cardinality answers where the
30	interesting dimension is a **tag**, not a field. Take a per-api-key request-rate measure: the
31	user is the `service_id` tag, the api-key is the `entity_id` tag, and the only field is a scalar
32	request count. Three questions follow immediately.
33	
34	| Case | Question | SQL shape |
35	|---|---|---|
36	| **Scalar** | "how many distinct api-keys did one user use last week?" | `COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) WHERE service_id = …` over a multi-bucket window |
37	| **Ranked** | "show every user, ranked by key count, page 3" | `GROUP BY service_id`, `ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) DESC`, `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` |
38	| **Series** | "plot distinct api-keys per 5 minutes for the last hour" | `GROUP BY <time bucket>, service_id ORDER BY <time bucket> ASC` |
39	
40	The ranked case is what a dashboard row needs; the series case is what a dashboard *chart* needs.
41	Every realistic dashboard window spans many buckets, so the scalar case is never asked over a
42	single bucket either.
43	
44	The series case is the shape analytical SQL expresses with a bucketing function — PostgreSQL and
45	DataFusion spell it `DATE_BIN(INTERVAL <width>, time, <origin>)`, others `time_bucket` or
46	`GROUP BY FLOOR(time/width)`. The semantics this design adopts are that function's, with the
47	origin fixed at the Unix epoch: each row is assigned to `floor(timestamp / width) * width`, and
48	rows sharing a bucket and a tag key form one group.
49	
50	None of the three is expressible today.
51	
52	- `measurev1.QueryRequest.Aggregation` names only a **field**. `plan/analyzer.go:301
53	  validateAggField` walks `measureSchema.GetFields()` and rejects anything else.
54	- `modelv1.AggregationFunction` is `{MEAN, MAX, MIN, COUNT, SUM}` — there is no `COUNT_DISTINCT`.
55	- **There is no time bucketing anywhere in the measure query API.** `QueryRequest.GroupBy` is
56	  `{tag_projection, field_name}` — tags only; the timestamp is not addressable as a group key,
57	  and no interval/step/bin concept exists in `query.proto`. Worse, aggregation deliberately
58	  *discards* time: `buildAggOutputLayout` emits `[shard_id?] + tags + agg columns` with no
59	  `RoleTimestamp`, and `plan/build_test.go:221` pins it — *"aggregation output must drop
60	  timestamp (D2)"*. The row path agrees (`measure_plan_aggregation.go:286,342` build
61	  `DataPoint{TagFamilies: …}` and never set `Timestamp`). So `agg` collapses the entire
62	  `time_range` into one row per tag group, always.
63	
64	The workarounds all fail:
65	
66	1. **`COUNT(*)` over one bucket.** This leans on storage usually holding one row per
67	   `(entity, bucket)` — and `Measure.interval` is a **declared cadence, not an enforced
68	   invariant**. Writers may emit off-cadence: on a 1-minute measure, timestamps of `09:01:00`
69	   *and* `09:01:34` are both legal and both land in the 09:01 bucket. So the count can be wrong
70	   even inside a single bucket, and it is certainly wrong once the window spans two — measured at
71	   21 for 3 keys over 7 buckets. No error, just a plausible wrong number. This is the strongest
72	   argument for a real `COUNT_DISTINCT`: the shortcut it replaces has no invariant behind it,
73	   only a convention writers are free to break.
74	2. **`groupBy(entity_id)` and count rows client-side.** Correct at any window, but it ships one
75	   row per distinct value to the *client*, and it does not compose with `top` / `offset` /
76	   `limit`, so the ranked case cannot be rendered.
77	3. **One query per bucket.** Correct at any window — each individual query is the workaround-1
78	   shape, exact precisely because its window is one bucket wide — and it is the only workaround
79	   that still composes with ranking. The cost is a fan-out: a 1-hour window at 1-minute
80	   granularity is 60 round-trips, a day is 1440, and the caller carries the bucket arithmetic,
81	   the partial-failure handling and the reassembly.
82	
83	### 1.1 The driving requirement for time bucketing
84	
85	The series case is not a speculative extension of the cardinality work. It comes from a separate
86	requirement: converting existing analytical queries onto BanyanDB, where the canonical shape is
87	
88	> group by **a time bucket plus two or more tag dimensions**, select a `COUNT(DISTINCT <tag>)`
89	> over a further tag that is **not** carried as an output column, alias the result, and select
90	> additional aggregates alongside it in the same row.
91	
92	Read as a checklist, that shape is the fastest way to see what the design must cover:
93	
94	| Element of the shape | Requirement | Where |
95	|---|---|---|
96	| group by a time bucket | time-bucket group key, emitted as the row timestamp | §5.1, §7.2 |
97	| group by several tags as well | **multiple** tag group keys alongside the bucket | §5.1 |
98	| `COUNT(DISTINCT <tag>)` | `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a tag | §5.1, §7.4 |
99	| the distinct target is not an output column | target stripped from the output, not emitted as a first-seen tag | §5.2 |
100	| the result is aliased | a result alias | **out of scope** — §3 |
101	| further aggregates in the same row | more than one aggregate per request | **out of scope** — §3 |
102	
103	The last two rows are deliberately out of scope (§3). This design delivers the `COUNT_DISTINCT`
104	half of the shape; a caller converting such a query issues the distinct count as its own request
105	and names the result column client-side. That is a smaller step than the full conversion, and
106	saying so plainly is better than implying the checklist is fully served.
107	
108	Two further notes on mapping this query onto a measure:
109	
110	- **All group tags must live in one tag family.** `distributedGroupByTagNames`
111	  (`distributed.go:1131`) reads `families[0]` only, so the tag dimensions grouped alongside the
112	  bucket must share a family. This is a pre-existing v1 limitation, not one this design adds, but
113	  it constrains the schema the conversion targets.
114	- **The effective routing key determines whether the distinct pushes down** (§7.4) — the
115	  measure's `sharding_key` when set, otherwise its entity. The condition is
116	  `routingTags ⊆ groupByTags ∪ {target}`, so a routing key drawn from the grouped tags plus the
117	  distinct target pushes down; a routing tag outside that set gets the query rejected. A
118	  conversion gets to *choose* its routing key, so this is a modelling instruction rather than a
119	  constraint discovered too late.
120	- **The query must resolve to a single stage** (§7.4). Multi-stage `COUNT_DISTINCT` is rejected,
121	  and an empty `stages` falls back to `DefaultStages` — so this is a constraint on the target
122	  group's lifecycle configuration, not just on the query text.
123	
124	The gap is narrow and the engine already has every primitive needed to close it: grouping over
125	tag columns, a Map/Reduce split across data nodes and the liaison, a per-query memory budget,
126	top-N/pagination over an aggregate output column, and — for the series case — an
127	epoch-anchored bucketing formula already in the tree (`getWindowStart` in
128	`pkg/flow/streaming/sliding_window.go:302`, used by the TopN pre-aggregation path).
129	
130	**Time bucketing and tag aggregation are orthogonal**, and the series case needs both. They would
131	be near-interchangeable if a measure held exactly one row per `(entity, interval)` — then
132	counting rows in a bucket would count distinct entities. It does not: the interval is a declared
133	cadence, so two rows for one entity can share a bucket. `COUNT` grouped by bucket therefore
134	answers "how many data points", `COUNT_DISTINCT` answers "how many distinct things", and they
135	diverge whenever a writer emits off-cadence or a query bucket is coarser than the interval.
136	Shipping either feature alone leaves half the dashboard unservable.
137	
138	---
139	
140	## 2. Requirements
141	
142	- `agg` may target a **tag** as well as a field.
143	- A new `COUNT_DISTINCT` function, **exact** (not sketch-based).
144	- `group_by` may key on a **time bucket**, producing one row per `(bucket, tag group)` and a
145	  timestamp on each result row. The width comes from the request or from the measure's
146	  `interval` — see §5.3.
147	- Bucket grouping must **stream node-locally**: on the part path, live state is one bucket rather
148	  than the whole window, and a node emits a bucket as it closes instead of withholding until its
149	  scan ends (§7.2). This is a requirement rather than an optimisation — it is what makes a
150	  day-long query at 1-minute buckets viable at all. It is explicitly **not** an end-to-end
151	  pipelining promise: the liaison collects node frames before reducing them, so the *query*
152	  remains request/response even where the *operator* streams. Index mode does not stream at all
153	  (§7.2).
154	- All of the above compose with each other and with the existing `top`, `offset` and `limit`, in
155	  standalone **and** distributed deployments.
156	- A high-cardinality target must fail loudly against the per-query budget, never OOM a node.
157	- `COUNT_DISTINCT` **pushes down to the data nodes like every other function**, with a scalar
158	  partial. A request that cannot be pushed down is **rejected at analyze time** — there is no
159	  second, costlier execution path (§7.4).
160	- **`index_mode` measures are in scope** for both grouping and aggregation, on the same terms as
161	  part-backed measures (§7.4, §7.7).
162	- Reachable from BydbQL, not only from clients that hand-build a `QueryRequest`.
163	- Default behaviour is unchanged: a request with no `time_bucket` still collapses the whole
164	  `time_range`, exactly as today.
165	
166	## 3. Non-goals
167	
168	- **Approximate distinct (HyperLogLog).** Constant wire cost is attractive, but it needs a new
169	  partial wire type and an API contract about error bounds. The cardinality of the motivating
170	  case (api-keys per user) does not justify either. Revisit only if a deployment actually hits
171	  the budget.
172	
173	> **Decided:** the two entries below are out of scope. `COUNT_DISTINCT` is the piece of §1.1 this
174	> design delivers; the remaining elements of that query shape are deferred deliberately, not left
175	> open. A caller converting such a query issues the distinct count as its own request and names
176	> the result column client-side.
177	
178	- **Multiple aggregates in one request.** `QueryRequest.agg` stays singular and BydbQL keeps
179	  erroring on a second aggregate in `SELECT`. The operator is already plural — `AggSpec` is a
180	  slice and `BatchAggregation` loops over `a.aggs` — so if this is ever picked up the work is API
181	  and planning rather than execution, and it can be added as `repeated Aggregation` under a new
182	  field number without breaking the singular form.
183	- **Result aliases (`AS`).** No BydbQL `AS` production and no `Aggregation.output_name`. The
184	  result column keeps the naming rule in §5.2: it is named after the aggregation target.
185	- **Row-path parity.** See §8.
186	- **`COUNT_DISTINCT` in `TopNAggregation` pre-aggregation rules.** Rejected, not implemented.
187	- **Per-bucket `top`.** With `time_bucket` set, `top`/`offset`/`limit` stay **global** over the
188	  whole result set — one heap, exactly today's semantics. "Top 10 devices *in each* bucket" is
189	  the TopN RPC's job and already exists there: `TopNResponse.lists` is "a series topN lists
190	  ranked by timestamp". Redefining `top` per bucket would fork that semantics across two APIs.
191	  See §10 for the consequence this has for `limit`.
192	- **Bucket gap-filling.** Buckets with no data produce no row. Zero-filling a sparse series is a
193	  presentation concern and needs the client to know the expected bucket set anyway.
194	- **Arbitrary bucket origins.** Buckets are anchored at the Unix epoch, matching the `DATE_BIN`
195	  call above with `TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:00'`. A configurable origin is not in scope.
196	
197	**Current limitation, not a design decision: `group_by.time_bucket` requires `agg`.** This
198	document never states whether a *raw* bucketed `GroupBy` (`time_bucket` set, no `agg`) is
199	supported — it is written throughout as if `agg` is always present. Implementing §7.2 found a
200	concrete reason it cannot be, as things stand: the no-`agg` shape reuses `BatchAggregation`'s
201	empty-`AggSpec` output layout, which — unlike `BatchGroupByFirst`, the row-preserving raw-GroupBy
202	operator — does not carry the full input schema forward (it drops other fields, the series id,
203	and the version), and the distributed row-merge path has no bucket-aware counterpart either. The
204	analyzer rejects this combination explicitly (`plan.Analyze: time_bucket requires Agg`) rather
205	than shipping a silently-truncated result. Lifting this is legitimate future work, but it needs
206	schema-preservation and distributed-merge work of its own; it is not a small extension of the
207	`agg` case.
208	
209	---
210	
211	## 4. Background: how measure aggregation works today
212	
213	The vectorized engine is the default (`vectorized/measure/config.go DefaultConfig` → `Enabled:
214	true`); the row engine in `pkg/query/logical/measure` is explicitly marked *"Do not extend with
215	new features"* (`measure_analyzer.go:62-68`).
216	
217	**Standalone.** `plan.Analyze` builds a `GroupByAgg` node which `BuildOperators`
218	(`vectorized/measure/plan.go:61`) turns into one `BatchAggregation`. Group keys are encoded by
219	`appendKeyComponent` (`groupby.go:287`) — a shared helper that handles int64, float64, string,
220	bytes, `*modelv1.TagValue` and `*modelv1.FieldValue`. Each group holds one `aggSlot` per
221	aggregate, backed by `pkg/query/aggregation`.
222	
223	**Distributed.** The liaison sets `InternalQueryRequest.AggReturnPartial`
224	(`plan/distributed.go:474`), which the data node turns into `AggModeMap`
225	(`plan/dispatch.go:120-123`). The node emits typed-column *partials* — a `Partial{Value, Count}`
226	per group — serialized by `vectorized/measure/frame`. The liaison runs `AggModeReduce`
227	(`reduce.go:107 ReducePartialBatches`), deduplicating replicas on `(shard_id, group_key)` before
228	combining.
229	
230	Two structural facts this design leans on:
231	
232	- **Tag columns cross the wire fine.** The frame codec carries string and bytes columns with
233	  their family name intact (`frame/encode.go:65-69`, `decode.go:105-107`). The raw-GroupBy
234	  distributed path (`distributed.go:913 applyBatchGroupByFirstToRows`) already ships tag columns
235	  from data nodes and dedupes them liaison-side. Only array columns have no wire type
236	  (`frame/frame.go:185-202` → `ErrUnsupportedColumnType`).
237	- **A tag is only a *native typed* column when something keys off it.** `BuildBatchSchema`
238	  (`integration.go:60`) consults `buildNativeTagSet` (`:139`), which today contains only GroupBy
239	  keys. Every other tag stays a `ColumnTypeTagValue` passthrough. This matters because
240	  `aggregation.go:464 fold` hard-casts to `TypedColumn[int64]`/`[float64]` with no fallback.
241	
242	---
243	
244	## 5. API
245	
246	### 5.1 Proto
247	
248	One enum value in `api/proto/banyandb/model/v1/common.proto`:
249	
250	```proto
251	enum AggregationFunction {
252	  …
253	  AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_SUM = 5;
254	  // COUNT_DISTINCT counts the distinct non-null values of the target.
255	  // It is exact and bounded by the per-query memory budget.
256	  AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_COUNT_DISTINCT = 6;
257	}
258	```
259	
260	One field on `QueryRequest.Aggregation` in `api/proto/banyandb/measure/v1/query.proto`:
261	
262	```proto
263	message Aggregation {
264	  model.v1.AggregationFunction function = 1;
265	  // field_name must be one of files indicated by the field_projection
266	  string field_name = 2;
267	  // tag_name aggregates over a tag instead of a field. Exactly one of
268	  // field_name and tag_name must be set.
269	  string tag_name = 3;
270	}
271	```
272	
273	One field on `QueryRequest.GroupBy`, in the same file:
274	
275	```proto
276	message GroupBy {
277	  // tag_projection must be a subset of the tag_projection of QueryRequest
278	  model.v1.TagProjection tag_projection = 1;
279	  // field_name must be one of fields indicated by field_projection
280	  string field_name = 2;
281	  message TimeBucket {
282	    // width is a duration string using the same units as Measure.interval
283	    // ("ns", "us", "ms", "s", "m", "h", "d"). Empty means "use the measure's
284	    // interval"; if the measure has no interval either, the request is
285	    // rejected.
286	    string width = 1;
287	  }
288	  // time_bucket adds the data point's timestamp, floored to a bucket boundary,
289	  // as the leading group key, and re-emits it as the result row's timestamp.
290	  // Buckets are anchored at the Unix epoch: bucket_start = ts - ts % width,
291	  // matching DATE_BIN with a Unix-epoch origin. Unset means no time bucketing
292	  // — the whole time_range collapses to one row per tag group, as today.
293	  TimeBucket time_bucket = 3;
294	}
295	```
296	
297	All additions are wire-compatible; existing clients are unaffected, and an unset `time_bucket`
298	preserves today's behaviour exactly.
299	
300	**The aggregation target is qualified by family.** An earlier draft used a bare `tag_name`,
301	reasoning that the engine keys tag specs by bare name
302	(`pkg/query/logical/schema.go:92-99`) and so names must be unique. That is an implementation
303	assumption, not a schema invariant — and the two are not the same thing. Tag-family validation
304	(`api/validate/validate.go:329-347`) does not reject a name repeated across families;
305	`pkg/pb/v1/metadata.go:27-35` makes the same unenforced assumption; and
306	`pkg/query/vectorized/schema_test.go:81-94` explicitly exercises identical names in different
307	families. `RegisterTag` silently overwrites one family's spec with another's.
308	
309	So a bare name can be ambiguous on a valid schema. Two ways out were available: retrofit a global
310	uniqueness rule, or qualify at the new seam. **Qualifying is the correct one** — a uniqueness
311	rule would invalidate existing schemas that are legal today, to serve a feature they do not use.
312	`GroupBy` already qualifies by family; the aggregation target now matches it.
313	
314	### 5.2 Result naming
315	
316	The result column **inherits the target's name**, extending the existing field rule
317	(`plan.go:109-116`, pinned by `plan_test.go
318	TestBuildOperators_AggOutputName_InheritsInputFieldName`). So
319	`COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id) GROUP BY service_id` returns tag `service_id` plus field `entity_id`,
320	and the ranked case orders with `top.field_name = "entity_id"` — no new API surface for ordering.
321	
322	When the analyzer injects the target tag into the tag projection itself (the caller did not ask
323	for it), that tag is **stripped from the output**. Otherwise every result row would also carry a
324	meaningless first-seen copy of the value being counted. If the caller *does* project the tag
325	explicitly, they get both a tag and a field of that name; the two live in separate namespaces
326	(`BatchSchema.tagByPath`, keyed by `(family, name)`, vs `fieldByName`) so nothing collides.
327	
328	The bucket has no such naming question: it is carried on `DataPoint.timestamp`, a field the
329	message already has, set to the **bucket start**. There is no synthetic `time_bucket` tag or
330	field — the wire shape of a bucketed result is the wire shape of any other data point.
331	
332	### 5.3 Resolving the bucket width
333	
334	The width comes from the request, or failing that from the measure. Either source is enough;
335	only the absence of both is an error.
336	
337	| `time_bucket` | `Measure.interval` | Outcome |
338	|---|---|---|
339	| unset | — | No bucketing. Today's behaviour, unchanged. |
340	| set, `width` given | — | Bucket width = `width`. |
341	| set, `width` empty | set | Bucket width = the measure's interval. |
342	| set, `width` empty | empty | **Reject** — *"time_bucket needs a width: measure %q declares no interval"*. |
343	| set, `width` unparseable / zero / negative | — | Reject. |
344	
345	Both sources are parsed with `timestamp.ParseDuration` (`pkg/timestamp/duration.go:31`), the same
346	parser the write path uses on the schema field (`banyand/measure/measure.go:118`), so the two
347	agree on units by construction.
348	
349	**There is deliberately no "must be a multiple of the interval" rule.** An earlier draft required
350	one, on the reasoning that a narrower or non-aligned bucket would partition the data
351	arbitrarily. That reasoning assumed `Measure.interval` describes where data points actually land
352	— and it does not. The field declares a *cadence writers are asked to follow*, not an invariant
353	storage enforces: on a 1-minute measure, timestamps of `09:01:00` and `09:01:34` are both legal.
354	
355	Once points may fall anywhere, every width is equally meaningful — binning arbitrary timestamps
356	is exactly what `DATE_BIN` does — and a multiple-of rule would reject useful queries to protect
357	an alignment that was never guaranteed. What survives from that reasoning is a cost observation
358	rather than a constraint: bucket count is `time_range / width`, so a very small width against a
359	long window produces many groups. That is bounded by the memory budget (§7.6) and by `limit`
360	(§10), which is where cost belongs.
361	
362	The same correction removes an assumption that ran deeper than this section — see §1 on why
363	`COUNT(*)` is unreliable even within a single bucket, and §11 on the test that assumption would
364	have produced.
365	
366	### 5.4 BydbQL
367	
368	```sql
369	SELECT service_id, COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) FROM MEASURE … GROUP BY service_id
370	SELECT host, COUNT(host) FROM MEASURE … GROUP BY TIME_BUCKET('5m'), host
371	```
372	
373	`DISTINCT` is accepted inside `COUNT` only; `SUM(DISTINCT …)` is a parse error. The aggregate
374	column resolves against tags as well as fields — `transformer.go:846 convertAggregation`
375	currently hard-errors when the column is not in `allFields`.
376	
377	`TIME_BUCKET(<duration>)` is a pseudo-column accepted only in `GROUP BY`, at most once, and it
378	maps to `GroupBy.time_bucket`. The argument may be omitted — `TIME_BUCKET()` requests bucketing
379	at the measure's own interval, the `width`-empty case in §5.3. It is deliberately not selectable
380	in the projection: the bucket arrives on the data point's timestamp, not as a column. Results are
381	ordered by bucket ascending (§7.5), so an explicit `ORDER BY` on the bucket is unnecessary.
382

384	
385	## 6. Semantics
386	
387	Validated at analyze time; anything outside the matrix is a hard error naming the target and its
388	type.
389	
390	| Target type | SUM / MIN / MAX / MEAN | COUNT | COUNT_DISTINCT |
391	|---|---|---|---|
392	| Field INT / FLOAT | ✅ today | ✅ today | ✅ new |
393	| Tag `TAG_TYPE_INT` | ✅ new | ✅ new | ✅ new |
394	| Tag `TAG_TYPE_STRING` | ❌ reject | ✅ new | ✅ new |
395	| Tag `TAG_TYPE_DATA_BINARY` | ❌ reject | ✅ new | ✅ new |
396	| Tag `*_ARRAY`, `TAG_TYPE_TIMESTAMP` | ❌ reject | ❌ reject | ❌ reject |
397	
398	- Null values are excluded, matching the current field behaviour: they do not increment `COUNT`
399	  and do not enter the distinct set.
400	- `MEAN` over an INT tag yields float64, matching the existing field rule.
401	- **Array and timestamp tags must be rejected explicitly, not left to fall through.**
402	  `tagTypeToColumnType` (`integration.go:162`) already errors on `TIMESTAMP`, but array tags map
403	  to `ColumnTypeInt64Array`/`ColumnTypeStrArray`, and `appendKeyComponent`
404	  (`groupby.go:287-303`) *silently returns the buffer unchanged* for those — every row would
405	  collapse into one group and produce a plausible wrong count, the exact failure mode this
406	  design exists to remove. A `keyComponentSupported(ColumnType) bool` predicate should sit next
407	  to `appendKeyComponent` so the analyzer's rejection list and the operator's assumption cannot
408	  drift apart.
409	
410	Time bucketing is orthogonal to this matrix: it adds a group key, not an aggregate, so it
411	composes with every cell above. Its own validation rules are in §5.3. Two interactions are worth
412	stating explicitly:
413	
414	- **A bucket key does not change what an aggregate means** — it only narrows the row set each
415	  aggregate sees. `COUNT_DISTINCT` per bucket counts values distinct *within* that bucket; a
416	  value present in two buckets counts once in each. That is the intended series semantics, and it
417	  is deliberately not the same number as the unbucketed total.
418	- **`TAG_TYPE_TIMESTAMP` tags remain rejected** as aggregation targets. The bucket key comes from
419	  the data point's own timestamp, which is not a tag, so the two never meet.
420
